heading: INT. NIGHT BUS - LOWER DECK - NIGHT

units.text: INT. NIGHT BUS - LOWER DECK - NIGHT
London, fog thick as wet wool against the windows.
The bus lurches through an empty Bayswater, its engine groaning like an old man climbing stairs.
Edith Marsh, 30s, a nurse in a navy coat with the cap folded in her lap, sits near the back.
Her shoes are scuffed from a double shift.
Across the aisle, Walter Penn, 60s, a conductor with a ticket machine strapped to his chest, leans on the rail and yawns without apology.
ANGLE ON the dim bulb overhead, flickering, throwing yellow across faces.

Near the front, Alistair Crane, 40s, in a good tweed overcoat too warm for the night, reads a folded newspaper he is not reading, while beside him a boy, Tommy, 10, in a cap too big for him, kicks his heels against the seat and watches the rain run in lines down the glass, and Walter checks his watch and the clock above the driver and the road ahead, all in one practised sweep.
Fares, please. Fares. Last bus tonight, ladies and gentlemen. Last bus and last chance.
units.name: WALTER

units.text: You say that every night, Mr Penn.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: And every night I mean it, Miss Marsh.
units.name: WALTER

units.text: WE SEE Alistair's gloved hand tighten on the newspaper.
The boy has no ticket.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: Da says it's all right.
units.name: TOMMY

units.text: Does he.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: Where's your da, lad?
units.name: WALTER

units.text: Home. He's poorly.
units.name: TOMMY

units.text: Silence.
The bus turns a corner, and everyone sways together.
CLOSE ON Tommy's coat sleeve.
The cuff is worn through.
Edith sees it.
I'll pay his fare. Here. A tuppence, is it?
units.name: EDITH

units.text: Threepence from here, miss.
units.name: WALTER

units.text: Then threepence.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: She sets the coins in the machine's tray.
Alistair folds the newspaper at last, slow and exact, and looks at her for the first time.
That's very generous. I wonder you can afford it, on a nurse's wage.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: I wonder you can afford that coat, on whatever it is you do.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: Now then.
units.name: WALTER

units.text: I do very well, thank you. I take an interest in people who leave their patients at night.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: I haven't left anyone.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: Mrs Harcourt, in the end bed. She'd be a good deal more comfortable if you'd stayed.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: Edith goes still.
The engine drones.
Tommy has stopped kicking.
BACK TO SCENE: the bus slows at a stop where no one waits, the doors hiss, and cold air comes in carrying the smell of coal smoke.
Who are you?
units.name: EDITH

units.text: Someone who reads the ward reports.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: I think, sir, you'd best get off here.
units.name: WALTER

units.text: I think I'll ride to the terminus, conductor. I've paid.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: Miss, is he a policeman?
units.name: TOMMY

units.text: No, love. I think he's only lonely.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: Alistair's face flickers, the tiniest crack.
He looks at the boy, then at the fogged window, then at his own reflection, which looks like someone he would rather not be.
Mrs Harcourt died at nine. I was her son.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: I'm so sorry. I didn't know.
units.name: EDITH

units.text: No. Nobody did. She said you were kind.
units.name: ALISTAIR

units.text: Walter takes off his cap.
The doors hiss shut.
The bus pulls away into the fog, and no one says anything else.
